As a powerful tool to alleviate the data sparsity and cold-start problems in traditional recommender systems, cross-domain recommendation hinges on addressing two fundamental questions: how to transfer knowledge and what to transfer. Regarding the two questions, existing methods have limitations, such as restricted domain connections, inadequate representation disentanglement, and insufficient knowledge transfer. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel model, KDCLM, which integrates sophisticated knowledge distillation and contrastive learning mechanisms within a multi-view graph architecture. The proposed model comprises two views-a local view and a global view-both of which construct multiple graphs based on user-item interactions to establish richer domain connections. Specifically, the local view incorporates two contrastive learning mechanisms: one for aligning domain-invariant representations and another for differentiating domain-specific representations, which jointly achieve effective representation disentanglement. Syst. 44, 2, Article 40 (December 2025), 31 pages. https://doi.org/10.1145/3777418 ## 1 Introduction Recommender systems are designed to offer tailored suggestions of items that users might find interesting, based on their historical interactions, which are essential for tackling the issue of information overload. However, traditional recommender systems often struggle with data sparsity and the cold-start problem, which persistently hinder their effectiveness. With the increasing number of users engaging across multiple domains, such as movies and books, cross-domain recommendation (CDR) has garnered significant attention. The essence of CDR is to leverage information from various domains to mitigate the aforementioned issues. When designing a CDR method, two core issues need to be addressed: how to transfer and what to transfer. How to transfer focuses on establishing linkages between domains to facilitate knowledge transfer. Previous work typically begins by learning representations independently within each domain, followed by a direct integration of user representations from these domains to form the final representations [40, 80, 81]. However, given that different domains may possess distinct semantic spaces, these direct-integration methods can lead to issues such as feature conflicts. To address this, Man et al. [43] proposed an embedding and mapping framework, in which a mapping function between domains is learned to transfer source-domain user representations to the target domain. Li and Tuzhilin [29] proposed to learn a latent orthogonal mapping function across the two domains to preserve similarities of user preferences. Liu et al. [39] further incorporated differentially private projection to ensure effective and reliable knowledge transfer across domains. In contrast to these mapping-based methods, some researchers [18, 78] proposed constructing a cross-domain graph to model interactions in different domains as a whole and generate representations of both users and items within the same semantic space. What to transfer involves extracting valuable knowledge from each domain to be transferred across domains. Existing CDR methods can be categorized into two primary strategies: a blended strategy and a disentangled strategy [35]. Methods employing the blended strategy [36, 51, 60, 70] treat all information from other domains as knowledge to be transferred. However, as the transferred knowledge may contain domain-specific factors, this strategy can introduce noise, leading to negative transfer and decreased model performance. To avoid such negative transfer, methods based on the disentangled strategy have been proposed. For example, Yan et al. [67] proposed dividing user embeddings into a domain-shared part and a domain-specific part, treating the domain-shared part as the knowledge to be transferred across domains. Cao et al. [5] employed the Kullback-Leibler divergence distance to enforce the disentanglement of user features. Kong et al. [24] explored the disentanglement of domain information from a causality perspective and used a domain classifier with a gradient reverse layer to extract domain-shared information. Additionally, contrastive learning-based regularization terms \( \left\lbrack {1,{32},{74}}\right\rbrack \) have been widely proposed to maximize the mutual information of disentangled representations.

Despite their proven effectiveness, existing CDR methods still face three significant limitations in addressing the core issues of how to transfer and what to transfer: - Restricted Domain Connections: As shown in Figure 1(a), existing methods generally rely on overlapping users or auxiliary tags to bridge domains. However, in real scenarios, the overlap between domains is typically minimal [21] and auxiliary tags are often unavailable, making these methods impractical for real-world applications. - Inadequate Representation Disentanglement: When disentangling user interest representations, existing methods focus primarily on designing alignment strategies for domain-invariant parts of instances, while neglecting noise and redundancy in the generated representations (as illustrated in Figure 1(b)). This can lead to negative transfer and impair the representation abilities of user representations. - Insufficient Knowledge Transfer: Current approaches to knowledge transfer predominantly focus on different domains by incorporating user interest representations generated in other domains. To avoid negative transfer, only the domain-invariant part is utilized. However, this strategy is inherently limited. On the one hand, it ignores other rich and valuable information, such as graph signals (as shown in Figure 1(c)). On the other hand, it overlooked knowledge transfer between different views and different model structures. To address these limitations, we propose an innovative CDR model named KDCLM, which integrates sophisticated Knowledge distillation and Contrastive Learning techniques within a Multiview graph architecture. The proposed KDCLM model encompasses both a local view and a global view, responsible for user preference modeling within each domain and cross domains, respectively. In the local view, we construct user-item interaction graphs based on single-domain interactions. Domain-specific and domain-invariant interest representations for users are generated by employing stacked graph convolutional layers followed by two separate projection operations. To reduce noise and redundancy within the generated representations and achieve effective disentanglement, we design two contrastive learning mechanisms: an instance-level neighbor-discrimination mechanism to align domain-invariant representations and a feature-level mechanism to differentiate domain-specific representations. In the global view, we construct a heterogeneous user-item interaction graph based on cross-domain interactions, as well as homogeneous user-user and item-item similarity graphs based on behavioral similarity. These graphs directly connect users and items across different domains, rather than relying solely on overlapping users, thus facilitating richer domain connections. We then employ knowledge distillation (KD) to harness the complementary knowledge embedded in the graph signals from both heterogeneous and homogeneous graphs for sufficient knowledge transfer. The final recommendations are generated by fusing representations from both the local and global views.

The contributions of our work are summarized as follows: - We propose an innovative model, KDCLM, which effectively addresses the two core issues in CDR-what to transfer and how to transfer-through KD and contrastive learning techniques within a multi-view graph architecture. - We pioneer the simultaneous design of instance-level and feature-level contrastive learning mechanisms for representation disentanglement in CDR, achieving alignment of domain-invariant representations while differentiating domain-specific representations. - We leverage KD to fully exploit the complementary knowledge embedded in both heterogeneous and homogeneous global graphs, thereby maximizing the utilization of rich information encapsulated within graph signals. -Through comprehensive experiments on four CDR tasks, we demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed KDCLM model compared to state-of-the-art methods. The remainder of this article is organized as follows. After surveying related work in Section 2, we introduce notations and problem definition in Section 3. Section 4 details our proposed KDCLM model. Section 5 provides model analysis, including the training process and space-time complexity. Subsequently, experimental settings and results are presented in Section 6. Finally, we conclude this article in Section 7. ## 2 Related Work In this section, we introduce related work on CDR, graph neural network (GNN)-based recommender systems, contrastive learning for recommendation, and KD. ### 2.1 CDR CDR leverages information from multiple domains to alleviate data sparsity and cold-start problems in a target domain [73]. The core challenge in CDR lies in effectively transferring knowledge between domains. Early methods focused on direct knowledge transfer. Singh et al. first applied collective matrix factorization (CMF) [51] to CDR, jointly factorizing interaction matrices from both domains and sharing representations of common users. Hu et al. [17] proposed the collaborative cross-network, enabling dual knowledge transfer across domains through cross-connections between base networks. This dual transfer framework has been widely adopted and improved upon by subsequent researchers [29, 36, 37]. Zhu et al. introduced dual target cross-domain recommendation (DTCDR) [80], generating embeddings of users and items in each domain and combining overlapping user embeddings using various methods [81]. Man et al. proposed the embedding and mapping framework (EMCDR) [43] for cross-domain cold-start recommendation, learning a mapping function across domains using overlapping user representations. Meng et al. proposed the AMLCDR model [45], which includes a meta-learning network and a transfer network to reduce user preference loss, as well as a domain adaptation network to align user preference distribution. However, these methods directly transfer user interest representations from one domain to another, potentially introducing irrelevant information and degrading model performance through negative transfer. To address this, Yan et al. [67] first highlighted the importance of distinguishing between cross-domain commonality and domain peculiarity in user interests. Their method generates user representations with both domain-shared and domain-specific parts, tailored to individual users. Since then, numerous studies have focused on disentangling domain-shared and domain-specific information to avoid negative transfer. For example, Cao et al. proposed DisenCDR [5], which uses a variational bipartite graph encoder and mutual-information-based regularizes to disentangle user preferences. Zhu et al. introduced DIDA-CDR [82], training a domain classifier to generate domain-invariant features by making the classifier unable to identify the domain of the features. More recently, contrastive learning has been applied for representation disentanglement. Zang et al. [74] applied it to disentangle general interests in cross-domain sequential recommendation. Li et al. proposed MITrans [32], which realizes preference disentanglement even without overlapping users. Liu et al. [35] incorporated both user and item features into mutual-information calculations. However, these methods only adopt instance-level contrastive learning while our proposed model further incorporate feature-level contrastive learning to guarantee the differentiation of domain-specific representations in a finer-grained way.

### 2.2 GNN-Based Recommender Systems GNNs recursively propagate and aggregate messages among neighbors on graphs, capturing high-order relationships between nodes. This capability has made GNNs widely applicable in recommender systems. NGCF [57] was the first to adopt GNN-based collaborative filtering, learning user and item embeddings on the user-item interaction graph. Subsequent research has focused on improving the message propagation process and developing GNN paradigms tailored for recommendation. For example, Chen et al. proposed the GCCF model [7], which removes non-linear activations to enhance model performance with reduced complexity. It also learns residual user-item preferences at each layer to mitigate the over-smoothing problem. He et al. introduced LightGCN [13], which simplifies NGCF by removing feature transformation and non-linear activation, retaining only the most essential neighborhood aggregation component. Mao et al. proposed UltraGCN [44], an ultra-simplified graph convolutional network (GCN) model that directly approximates the limit of infinite-layer graph convolutions via a constraint loss, replacing explicit message passing. Wang et al. proposed DGCF [58], which constructs intent-aware graphs to disentangle representations of users and items at the granularity of user intents. Recent studies, such as SGL [62], SimGCL [72], and LightGCL [2], have further enhanced GNN-based recommender systems by incorporating contrastive learning. In the field of CDR, some studies leverage GNNs as single-domain information encoders to generate more informative embeddings in each domain [37, 38, 64, 69, 81]. Zhao et al. proposed Preference Propagation GraphNet [78], which constructs a cross-domain graph to model interactions across different domains as a whole. Guo et al. adopted a similar approach in cross-domain sequential recommendation [11]. Wang et al. then proposed the \( {I}^{2}\mathrm{{RCDR}} \) method [55],which constructs a cross-domain heterogeneous graph to preserve inter-domain relations, as well as two single-domain graphs to capture user-item interactions within each domain. DGML [59] also builds both single-domain and cross-domain graphs to extract domain-specific and domain-shared features. Cao et al. further proposed \( {C}^{2} \) DSR [3],which utilizes GNNs to jointly mine inter-sequence and intra-sequence item sequential signals. However, these GNN-based CDR methods primarily rely on overlapping users to construct cross-domain graphs. Given the small proportion of overlapping users in real-world datasets, the domain connections of these methods are significantly restricted.

### 2.3 Contrastive Learning for Recommendation Contrastive learning generates additional supervised signals directly from the data itself, enabling deep learning-based models to learn from unlabeled data. This approach has been widely adopted to address data sparsity issues across various fields, including machine learning [10, 15], computer vision [8, 19], and natural language processing [16, 63]. Given its effectiveness in downstream recommendation tasks, contrastive learning has been broadly applied to diverse recommendation scenarios. These including general recommendation [72, 75], sequential recommendation [56, 77], bundle recommendation [42, 65], social recommendation [41, 47], and cold-start recommendation [79]. Typically, contrastive learning-based recommendation methods start by creating different views through data augmentation. They then learn multiple representations from these views using various encoders. The contrastive loss is designed to enhance the consistency between positive sample pairs (i.e., the same instances from different views) while reducing the similarity among negative samples (i.e., distinct instances in different views). As for CDR, Xie et al. first proposed the CCDR model [64], which generates node representations by sampling subgraphs of each node on the whole graph and then maximizes the mutual information between overlapping user representations through contrastive learning. Cao et al. introduced the \( {C}^{2} \) DSR model [3],which maximizes the mutual information between single-domain sequences and original cross-domain sequences while minimizing the mutual information between single-domain sequences and augmented cross-domain sequences. Lu et al. proposed CL-DTCDR [40], which includes an intra-domain contrastive learning task to maximize the agreement between embeddings learned from different data, as well as an inter-domain task that maximizes the agreement between users' embeddings and their most similar users. Yang et al. propose UCLR [68], which incorporates user-aware contrastive learning with automatic temperature individualization to adaptively adjust the penalty strength for negative samples. Zhang et al. [76], Liu et al. [35], and Zang et al. [74] designed cross-domain contrastive learning objectives to disentangle domain-specific and domain-invariant representations. Different from the aforementioned work, in this article, we jointly propose an instance-level contrastive learning mechanism and a feature-level contrastive learning mechanism to align domain-invariant representations and differentiate domain-specific representations, respectively. This dual approach reduces noise and redundancy in the generated representations, thereby achieving effective disentanglement. ### 2.4 KD KD was initially proposed for model compression, typically involving a complex teacher model with large capacity and a compact student model. The student model is trained to mimic the teacher model to improve its performance, thereby achieving a balance between effectiveness and efficiency. KD has been widely applied in the field of computer vision, including application in image classification [33, 48], object detection [30, 50], and video segmentation [12, 46]. Inspired by the success of KD in computer vision, recent researchers have introduced KD into recommender systems to enhance model performance [6, 26, 61]. For instance, Tang and Wang first proposed ranking distillation [52], where the large teacher model provides top-K ranked unlabeled samples as extra training data, and the small student model learns from both the training set and the top-K samples generated by the teacher model. Lee et al. further proposed collaborative distillation [25], which samples both high- and low-ranked items in a probabilistic manner to learn both positive and negative correlations among items. Kang et al. proposed a DE-RRD method [20] that distills both the latent knowledge stored in the teacher model and the knowledge revealed from the teacher's predictions. They further proposed a HetComp method [22] that dynamically constructs knowledge to guide the student model in an easy-to-hard sequence. Liu et al. introduced an SGFD method [34] to extract effective recommendation-oriented features from generic modality features using the teacher-student framework.

Beyond model compression, some studies have utilized KD for knowledge transfer between models with different data sources. For example, Tao et al. proposed a distillation-enhanced social graph network [53] that transfers knowledge between the user-item bipartite graph and the user-user social graph. Ren et al. proposed a distillation-enhanced graph masked autoencoder [49] for bundle recommendation, transferring higher-order relations among users and bundles from the bundle view to the item view. Du et al. presented ensemble modeling with contrastive KD for sequential recommendation (EMKD) [9], which adopts KD to facilitate knowledge transfer between parallel sequence encoders. Li et al. further incorporated KD with large language models (LLMs) and proposed a prompt distillation approach [28] that distills knowledge from discrete prompts into continuous prompt vectors. In the context of CDR, Yang et al. proposed a multi-modal optimal transport knowledge distillation method [69] that constructs multi-layer KD between source and target domain classifiers. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to apply KD to harness the complementary knowledge embedded in the graph signals, thereby facilitating sufficient knowledge transfer in CDR. ## 3 Notations and Problem Definition we consider two distinct domains, \( {D}^{A} \) and \( {D}^{B} \) ,which share a common set of users denoted by \( \mathcal{U} \) . Each domain has its own unique set of items: \( {\mathcal{I}}^{A} \) for \( {D}^{A} \) and \( {\mathcal{I}}^{B} \) for \( {D}^{B} \) ,ensuring no overlap between the item sets. The interactions between users and items in these domains are represented by two binary matrices, \( {\mathbf{R}}^{A} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{\left| \mathcal{U}\right| \times \left| {\mathcal{I}}^{A}\right| } \) and \( {\mathbf{R}}^{B} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{\left| \mathcal{U}\right| \times \left| {\mathcal{I}}^{B}\right| } \) . Here, \( \left| \mathcal{U}\right| ,\left| {\mathcal{I}}^{A}\right| \) ,and \( \left| {\mathcal{I}}^{B}\right| \) represent the number of users and items in each domain,respectively. An entry \( {R}_{u,i} = 1 \) in these matrices signifies that user \( u \) has interacted with item \( i \) ,while \( {R}_{u,i} = 0 \) indicates the absence of such an interaction. Table 1 provides a summary of the notations used throughout this article. Given the interaction matrices \( {\mathbf{R}}^{A} \) and \( {\mathbf{R}}^{B} \) ,along with the user set \( \mathcal{U} \) and item sets \( {\mathcal{I}}^{A} \) and \( {\mathcal{I}}^{B} \) ,our objective is to enhance the recommendation quality for all users across both domains. Specifically,we aim to identify sets of items \( {\mathcal{I}}_{a} \subseteq {\mathcal{I}}^{A} \) and \( {\mathcal{I}}_{b} \subseteq {\mathcal{I}}^{B} \) that users have not yet interacted with but are likely to find appealing. ## 4 Proposed KDCLM Model The architecture of our proposed KDCLM model, as illustrated in Figure 2, comprises three main components: a local view, a global view, and a prediction layer. The local view constructs user-item interaction graphs in each domain and is equipped with a representation disentanglement module. The global view constructs a heterogeneous user-item interaction graph and two homogeneous graphs-user-user similarity and item-item relationship graphs-enhanced by a graph knowledge enhancement module. The prediction layer generates the final recommendation results. We will elaborate on these components in detail below. ### 4.1 Multi-View Graph Construction To effectively capture high-order and non-linear relationships between users and items, we leverage graph structures to enhance recommendation performance. Specifically, in addition to the widely used heterogeneous user-item interaction graphs, we construct two homogeneous graphs: global user-user similarity and item-item relationship graphs. These graphs directly connect users and items across different domains, enabling cross-domain knowledge transfer through multiple pathways rather than relying solely on overlapping users. This enables richer connections between the two domains.

Specifically, we employ LightGCN [13], a widely adopted GCN that has demonstrated effectiveness in previous studies. Let the embedding matrix of the \( l \) th layer be \( {\mathbf{E}}^{*,l} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{{N}^{ * } \times d} \) ,where \( * \in \{ {UI},{UU},{II},A,B\} \) denotes different graphs, \( {N}^{ * } \) is the number of nodes in graph \( {G}^{ * } \) ,and \( d \) is the embedding size. The initial embeddings \( {e}_{u}^{*,0} \) and \( {e}_{i}^{*,0} \) are treated as learnable parameters. By stacking \( L \) graph convolution layers and concatenating the embeddings generated at each layer, we obtain the final user and item representations in each graph:

\[{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{ * } = {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{*,\left( 0\right) }\left| \right| {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{*,\left( 1\right) }\left| \right| \ldots \left| \right| {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{*,\left( L\right) },\;{\mathbf{e}}_{i}^{ * } = {\mathbf{e}}_{i}^{*,\left( 0\right) }\left| \right| {\mathbf{e}}_{i}^{*,\left( 1\right) }\left| \right| \ldots \left| \right| {\mathbf{e}}_{i}^{*,\left( L\right) }. \tag{3}\] Considering all constructed graphs,the resulting representations are as follows: for users, \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{UI} \) , \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{UU},{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{A} \) ,and \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{B} \) ; and for items in domain \( {D}^{A},{\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{A}}^{UI},{\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{A}}^{II} \) ,and \( {\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{A}}^{A} \) ; or for items in domain \( {D}^{B},{\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{B}}^{UI},{\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{B}}^{II} \) , and \( {\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{B}}^{B} \) . ### 4.3 Representation Disentanglement In CDR, user interests are composed of both domain-invariant factors-such as preferences for price and theme-and domain-specific factors-such as admiration for a particular actor in the Movies domain or preferences for certain melodies in the Music domain. Effectively disentangling these complex factors in the generated representations is pivotal for enhancing CDR performance. However, current methods, which predominantly focus on aligning domain-invariant features, often result in redundant and noisy representations due to inadequate disentanglement. This not only diminishes the representational capacity but also potentially introduces negative transfer, thereby undermining recommendation accuracy. To address these challenges, this article proposes a sophisticated mechanism for effective representation disentanglement. 4.3.1 Separate Representation Generation. To disentangle user interest representations, it is essential to generate separate embeddings that capture both domain-specific and domain-invariant factors. In our approach,we map the user representations \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{A} \) and \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{B} \) ,generated from the two local-view graphs, into two distinct semantic spaces using the following mapping functions: (4) \[{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{A,d} = {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{A} \odot \sigma \left( {{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{A}{\mathbf{W}}^{A,d} + {\mathbf{b}}^{A,d}}\right) ,\;{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{A,s} = {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{A} \odot \sigma \left( {{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{A}{\mathbf{W}}^{A,s} + {\mathbf{b}}^{A,s}}\right) ,\] \[{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{B,d} = {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{B} \odot \sigma \left( {{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{B}{\mathbf{W}}^{B,d} + {\mathbf{b}}^{B,d}}\right) ,\;{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{B,s} = {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{B} \odot \sigma \left( {{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{B}{\mathbf{W}}^{B,s} + {\mathbf{b}}^{B,s}}\right) ,\] where \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{A,d} \) and \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{B,d} \) represent the domain-invariant user representations,while \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{A,s} \) and \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{B,s} \) capture domain-specific information. Here, \( {\mathbf{W}}^{*,d} \) and \( {\mathbf{W}}^{*,s} \) are learnable projection heads, \( {\mathbf{b}}^{*,s} \) and \( {\mathbf{b}}^{*,d} \) are bias terms, \( * \in \{ A,B\} , \odot \) denotes element-wise multiplication,and \( \sigma \) is the sigmoid activation function. Since items are domain-specific and do not require disentanglement, this mechanism is applied exclusively to user representations. After generating these separate representations, the next crucial step is to optimize them efficiently to enforce disentanglement. To achieve this, we design two distinct contrastive learning objectives: one for the alignment of domain-invariant representations and another for the differentiation of domain-specific representations. In the following, we will elaborate on them. 4.3.2 Alignment of Domain-Invariant Representations. Since domain-invariant representations capture interests shared across domains, they should remain consistent for the same user across different domains. Contrastive learning, which is known for its capability to maximize agreement between positive samples while minimizing agreement between negative samples, has been widely adopted in CDR methods [35, 76]. Specifically, these methods typically treat domain-invariant representations of the same user as positive samples and representations of different users within the same batch as negative samples to align domain-invariant representations. However, this conventional self-discrimination contrastive learning approach (illustrated in the left side of Figure 3(a)) overlooks supervisory signals from similar users. Inspired by Yu et al. [71], we propose an innovative instance-level neighbor-discrimination contrastive learning approach (shown in the right side of Figure 3(a)) that leverages neighboring users to provide richer supervisory signals. To adaptively identify informative neighbors for each user, we consider both behavioral similarity and embedding similarity among users. Specifically, behavioral similarity is defined as the interaction of two users with at least one common item, while embedding similarity is inferred through a mixture-of-expert (MoE) architecture comprising \( P \) experts which infers embedding similarity of users from various aspects, identifying neighbors that carry similar information in different semantic spaces. Each expert \( p \) generates a similarity score for a user pair \( \left( {u,v}\right) \) to reflect its unique perspective:

\[{f}_{p}\left( {u,v}\right) = \frac{{\left( {\mathbf{w}}_{p} \odot {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{UU}\right) }^{T}\left( {{\mathbf{w}}_{p} \odot {\mathbf{e}}_{v}^{UU}}\right) }{{\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{w}}_{p} \odot {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{UU}\end{Vmatrix}}_{2} \cdot {\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{w}}_{p} \odot {\mathbf{e}}_{v}^{UU}\end{Vmatrix}}_{2}}, \tag{5}\] Fig. 3. Illustration of different contrastive learning paradigms. where \( {\mathbf{w}}_{p} \in {\mathbb{R}}^{d} \) is an expert-specific projection vector,enabling each expert to express diverse opinions,and \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{UU} \) and \( {\mathbf{e}}_{v}^{UU} \) are user representations generated from the global user-user similarity graph. The final similarity score is obtained by aggregating the opinions of different experts: \[{\widehat{S}}_{u,v} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{p = 1}}^{P}{\alpha }_{u,v}^{p}{f}_{p}\left( {u,v}\right) \tag{6}\] where \( {\alpha }_{u,v}^{p} \) denotes the weight of the \( p \) th expert,computed via a softmax operation: \( {\alpha }_{u,v}^{p} = \) softmax \( \left\{ {{\mathbf{W}}_{g}\cos \left( {{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{UU},{\mathbf{e}}_{v}^{UU}}\right) }\right\} \) . The neighbors of each user are then identified as follows: \[{\widetilde{S}}_{u,v} = \left\{ \begin{array}{ll} 1, & {\widehat{S}}_{u,v} \geq \delta \text{ or }{A}_{u,v}^{UU} = 1, \\ 0, & \text{ elsewise, } \end{array}\right. \tag{7}\] where \( \delta \) is a hyper-parameter serving as the threshold for embedding similarity,and \( {A}_{u,v}^{UU} = 1 \) indicates that users \( u \) and \( v \) have interacted with at least one common item. \( {\widetilde{S}}_{u,v} = 1 \) signifies that \( u \) and \( v \) are identified as neighbors. The neighbor-discrimination contrastive learning objective for domain \( {\mathcal{D}}^{A} \) is defined as: \[{\mathcal{L}}_{C{L}_{a}}^{A} = - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{u \in \mathcal{U}}}\left\lbrack {{log}\frac{\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{r \in \{ v \mid {\widetilde{S}}_{u,v} = 1\} }}\exp \left( {s\left( {{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{A,d},{\mathbf{e}}_{r}^{B,d}}\right) /\tau }\right) }{\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{r \in \{ v \mid {\widetilde{S}}_{u,v} = 1\} }}\exp \left( {s\left( {{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{A,d},{\mathbf{e}}_{r}^{B,d}}\right) /\tau }\right) + \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{t \in \{ v \mid {\widetilde{S}}_{u,v} = 0\} }}\exp \left( {s\left( {{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{A,d},{\mathbf{e}}_{r}^{B,d}}\right) /\tau }\right) }}\right\rbrack , \tag{8}\] where \( s\left( \cdot \right) \) is a function used to measure the similarity between two vectors. In this article,we adopt the widely used cosine similarity,defined as \( s\left( {{\mathbf{e}}_{1},{\mathbf{e}}_{2}}\right) = \left( {{\mathbf{e}}_{1}^{T} \cdot {\mathbf{e}}_{2}}\right) /\left( {\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{e}}_{1}\end{Vmatrix} \cdot \begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{e}}_{2}\end{Vmatrix}}\right) .\tau \) is a hyper-parameter for the softmax temperature,used to amplify the effect of discrimination. \( {\mathcal{L}}_{C{L}_{a}}^{B} \) can be similarly defined by swapping the symbols \( A \) and \( B \) in the above equation.

It is worth noting that as training progresses, user representations will improve the construction of better neighboring relationships, which in turn recursively benefit the generation of more effective user representations. In the initial epochs of training, since user representations are close to random initialization, we rely solely on behavioral similarity for neighbor identification, which we refer to as the warm-up phase. 4.3.3 Differentiation of Domain-Specific Representations. While the instance-level neighbor-discrimination contrastive learning mechanism described above is effective, it still has two potential limitations in representation disentanglement. First, it only maximizes the agreement between a user's domain-invariant representations across domains but cannot guarantee that all domain-invariant factors are fully captured in these representations. This may lead to insufficient or even negative knowledge transfer. Second, it imposes no constraints on domain-specific representations, which may retain redundancy and fail to fully capture the unique characteristics of each domain. Therefore, it is crucial to further enhance the differentiation of domain-specific representations to overcome these deficiencies. Unlike the alignment of domain-invariant representations, which focuses on instance-level consistency, the differentiation of domain-specific representations emphasizes feature-wise diversity (illustrated in Figure 3(b)). To address the limitations of the instance-level approach, we introduce a feature-level contrastive learning objective inspired by Zhang et al. [75]. Specifically, we use a polynomial kernel \( K\left( {x,y}\right) = {\left( x \cdot y + c\right) }^{e} \) to promote uniformity on the hyper-sphere: \[{\mathcal{L}}_{C{L}_{d}} = \log \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{m,n}}K\left( {{\left( {\mathbf{U}}_{A}^{ : ,m}\right) }^{\top },{\mathbf{U}}_{B}^{ : ,n}}\right) + \log \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{m \neq n}}K\left( {{\left( {\mathbf{U}}_{A}^{ : ,m}\right) }^{\top },{\mathbf{U}}_{A}^{ : ,n}}\right) + \log \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{m \neq n}}K\left( {{\left( {\mathbf{U}}_{B}^{ : ,m}\right) }^{T},{\mathbf{U}}_{B}^{ : ,n}}\right)\] \[= \log \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{m,n}}{\left( {\left( {\mathbf{U}}_{A}^{ : ,m}\right) }^{T}{\mathbf{U}}_{B}^{ : ,n} + c\right) }^{e} + \log \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{m \neq n}}{\left( {\left( {\mathbf{U}}_{A}^{ : ,m}\right) }^{T}{\mathbf{U}}_{A}^{ : ,n} + c\right) }^{e} + \log \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{m \neq n}}{\left( {\left( {\mathbf{U}}_{B}^{ : ,m}\right) }^{T}{\mathbf{U}}_{B}^{ : ,n} + c\right) }^{e}, \tag{9}\] where \( {\mathbf{U}}_{A} \) and \( {\mathbf{U}}_{B} \) denote the domain-specific user representations in \( {\mathcal{D}}^{A} \) and \( {\mathcal{D}}^{B} \) . Each inner-product term \( {\left( {\mathbf{x}}^{\top }\mathbf{y} + c\right) }^{e} \) is exactly the polynomial kernel value \( K\left( {x,y}\right) \) ,so Equation (9) can be interpreted as summing the kernel similarities between all required pairs and then taking the logarithm for numerical stability. The first term encourages differentiation between a user's domain-specific representations across different domains, effectively pushing domain-invariant factors into the domain-invariant representations. The subsequent two terms aim to reduce redundancy within each user's domain-specific representation of each domain, thereby preserving more semantic information. By minimizing \( {\mathcal{L}}_{C{L}_{d}} \) ,we further disentangle user representations,enhancing both the sufficiency of knowledge transfer and the distinctiveness of domain-specific information. ### 4.4 Graph Knowledge Enhancement In contrast to the representation disentanglement module, which focuses on aligning domain-invariant representations and differentiating domain-specific representations within the local view, the graph knowledge enhancement module aims to facilitate sufficient knowledge transfer in the global view by leveraging insights from graph signals. After multi-view representation learning, for each user \( u \) ,we generate two global representations: \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{UI} \) from the heterogeneous user-item interaction graph \( {G}^{UI} \) and \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{UU} \) from the homogeneous user-user similarity graph \( {G}^{UU} \) . Similarly, for each item \( {i}_{A} \) (or \( {i}_{B} \) ),we obtain two global representations: \( {\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{A}}^{UI}\left( {\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{B}}^{UI}\right) \) and \( {\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{A}}^{II}\left( {\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{B}}^{II}\right) \) from \( {G}^{UI} \) and \( {G}^{II} \) ,respectively. Although these graphs model users and items from a global perspective,the generated representations exhibit different characteristics due to separate modeling and diverse graph properties. To capitalize on the complementary knowledge from both heterogeneous and homogeneous graphs, we propose employing KD to further enhance model performance, the benefits of which are twofold: (i) The heterogeneous user-item graph encodes interaction signals, whereas the homogeneous user-user/item-item graphs encode similarity and structure signals. KD explicitly minimizes the mutual-information gap between these two modalities, ensuring knowledge consistency. (ii) Jointly training on graphs of different scales may cause gradient conflicts. KD treats the heterogeneous and homogeneous graphs as mutually regularizing soft targets, eliminating gradient interference. Specifically, KD is performed bidirectionally, with the heterogeneous and homogeneous graphs alternately acting as teacher and student models. The distillation loss is defined as follows:

\[{\mathcal{L}}_{KD}^{ * } = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{\left( u,{i}_{ * }\right) }\left( {{\mathcal{L}}_{CE}\left( {{\widetilde{y}}_{u,{i}_{ * }}^{E},{\widetilde{y}}_{u,{i}_{ * }}^{O}}\right) + {\mathcal{L}}_{CE}\left( {{\widetilde{y}}_{u,{i}_{ * }}^{O},{\widetilde{y}}_{u,{i}_{ * }}^{E}}\right) }\right) , \tag{10}\] where \( * \in \{ A,B\} \) indicates different domains, \( {\widetilde{y}}_{u,{i}_{ * }}^{E} = {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{U{I}^{T}}{\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{ * }}^{UI} \) and \( {\widetilde{y}}_{u,{i}_{ * }}^{O} = {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{U{U}^{T}}{\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{ * }}^{II} \) denote the preference probability scores calculated based on representations from the heterogeneous graph \( {G}^{UI} \) and the homogeneous graphs \( {G}^{UU} \) and \( {G}^{II} \) ,respectively. The binary cross-entropy loss \( {\mathcal{L}}_{CE}\left( {{y}_{S},{y}_{T}}\right) \) is defined as: \[{\mathcal{L}}_{CE}\left( {{y}_{S},{y}_{T}}\right) = - \left( {{y}_{T}\log \left( {y}_{S}\right) + \left( {1 - {y}_{T}}\right) \log \left( {1 - {y}_{S}}\right) }\right) , \tag{11}\] where \( {y}_{S} \) and \( {y}_{T} \) denote the outputs of the student model and the teacher model,respectively. ### 4.5 Prediction Layer After the aforementioned process, we obtain representations for users and items. Specifically, for each user \( u \) ,we derive global representations \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{UI} \) and \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{UU} \) ,as well as local interest representations \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{A,d} \) and \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{A,s} \) for domain \( {D}^{A} \) ,and \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{B,d} \) and \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{B,s} \) for domain \( {D}^{B} \) . Correspondingly,for each item \( i \) , we obtain representations \( {\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{A}}^{UI},{\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{A}}^{II} \) and \( {\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{A}}^{A} \) for domain \( {D}^{A} \) and \( {\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{B}}^{UI},{\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{B}}^{II} \) ,and \( {\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{B}}^{B} \) for domain \( {D}^{B} \) . We integrate these representations to form the final user and item representations as follows: (12) \[{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{{f}_{A}} = {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{UI}\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{UU}\end{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{A,d}\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{B,d}\end{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{A,s},\;{\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{A}}^{f} = {\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{A}}^{UI}\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{A}}^{II}\end{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{A}}^{A},\] \[{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{{f}_{B}} = {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{UI}\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{UU}\end{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{A,d}\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{B,d}\end{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{B,s},\;{\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{B}}^{f} = {\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{B}}^{UI}\begin{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{B}}^{II}\end{Vmatrix}{\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{B}}^{B},\] where || denotes concatenation. It is important to highlight that, despite a user being common across both domains, the distinct domain-specific interest representations result in different final representations for the same user in each domain (i.e., \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{{f}_{A}} \) and \( {\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{{f}_{B}} \) ). To estimate the interaction likelihood between each user-item pair \( \left( {u,i}\right) \) ,we generate predictions as follows: \[{\widehat{y}}_{ui}^{ * } = \sigma \left( {{\mathbf{W}}_{2}^{ * }\left( {\operatorname{ReLU}\left( {{\mathbf{W}}_{1}^{ * }\left\lbrack {{\mathbf{e}}_{u}^{{f}_{ * }},{\mathbf{e}}_{{i}_{ * }}^{f}}\right\rbrack + {\mathbf{b}}_{1}^{ * }}\right) }\right) + {\mathbf{b}}_{2}^{ * }}\right) , \tag{13}\] where \( * \in \{ A,B\} \) ,and the prediction process is consistent across both domains. Here, \( {\mathbf{W}}^{ * } \) and \( {\mathbf{b}}^{ * } \) are learnable parameters,and \( {\widehat{y}}_{ui}^{ * } \) denotes the predicted score,indicating the probability of user \( u \) interacting with item \( i \) . ### 4.6 Model Optimization We adopt cross-entropy as the recommendation loss for model training, with the specific formula given below: \[{\mathcal{L}}_{CE}^{ * } = - \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{\left( {u,i}\right) \in {\mathbf{R}}^{ + } \cup {\mathbf{R}}^{ - }}}{y}_{ui}^{ * }\log {\widehat{y}}_{ui}^{ * } + \left( {1 - {y}_{ui}^{ * }}\right) \log \left( {1 - {\widehat{y}}_{ui}^{ * }}\right) , \tag{14}\] where the symbol \( * \) can be replaced with either \( A \) or \( B \) to obtain the loss functions for domains \( {D}^{A} \) and \( {D}^{B} \) ,respectively,denoted as \( {\mathcal{L}}^{A} \) and \( {\mathcal{L}}^{B} \) . Here, \( {\mathbf{R}}^{ + } \) represents the set of observed user-item interactions,and \( {\mathbf{R}}^{ - } \) indicates the set of sampled negative instances.

Given the losses defined in Equations (8)-(10), the overall loss function is a composite of these components, formulated as follows: \[\mathcal{L} = {\mathcal{L}}_{CE}^{A} + {\mathcal{L}}_{CE}^{B} + {\lambda }_{1}\left( {{\mathcal{L}}_{KD}^{A} + {\mathcal{L}}_{KD}^{B}}\right) + {\lambda }_{2}\left( {{\mathcal{L}}_{C{L}_{a}}^{A} + {\mathcal{L}}_{C{L}_{a}}^{B} + {\mathcal{L}}_{C{L}_{d}}}\right) + {\lambda }_{3}\parallel \Theta {\parallel }_{2}^{2}, \tag{15}\] where \( {\lambda }_{1} \) and \( {\lambda }_{2} \) are coefficients that control the contributions of the KD and contrastive learning losses during model training. \( \Theta \) denotes the set of model parameters,and \( {L2} \) regularization is applied to \( \Theta \) with coefficient \( {\lambda }_{3} \) to prevent overfitting. ## 5 Model Analysis ### 5.1 Training Process The training of KDCLM is conducted using mini-batch gradient descent with the Adam optimizer, and model parameters are initialized via Xavier initialization. The training process begins by constructing two single-domain user-item interaction graphs, \( {G}^{A} \) and \( {G}^{B} \) ,in the local view,along with a cross-domain user-item interaction graph \( {G}^{UI} \) ,a user-user similarity graph \( {G}^{UU} \) ,and an item-item relationship graph \( {G}^{II} \) in the global view. Subsequently,representations of users and items are generated through graph convolution operations on \( {G}^{UI},{G}^{UU},{G}^{II},{G}^{A} \) and \( {G}^{B} \) ,as outlined in Equations (1)-(3). Next, domain-specific and domain-invariant user representations are derived using Equation (4). The neighbor-discrimination contrastive learning objective is defined for domain-invariant representation alignment, and the feature-level contrastive learning objective is employed for domain-specific representation differentiation, as specified in Equations (8) and (9). Specifically, during the initial epochs of training (i.e., the warm-up phase), neighbors are determined based on behavioral similarity. Afterward, neighbors are identified by jointly considering behavioral similarity and embedding similarity, as formulated in Equations (5)-(7). Moreover, preference probability scores are calculated based on the representations generated from \( {G}^{UI},{G}^{UU} \) ,and \( {G}^{II} \) ,and the KD loss is computed using Equations (10) and (11) to facilitate sufficient knowledge transfer. By combining representations from both the local and the global views, the final representations of users and items,denoted as \( {e}_{u}^{{f}_{A}},{e}_{u}^{{f}_{B}},{e}_{{i}_{A}}^{f} \) ,and \( {e}_{{i}_{B}}^{f} \) ,are obtained through Equation (12). The predicted interaction likelihood for each user-item pair is then generated using Equation (13). Finally, the cross-entropy loss in Equation (14) is adopted as the recommendation loss, and the overall loss function is derived by integrating all components, as presented in Equation (15). ### 5.2 Model Complexity We next discuss the scalability and efficiency of our proposed KDCLM model through a detailed space-time complexity analysis. 5.2.1 Space Complexity. The parameters of the KDCLM model consist of four distinct components: user and item embeddings, mapping functions used to generate separate representations, parameters within the MoE architecture for computing embedding similarities, and parameters in the prediction layer for generating predicted scores. The space complexities of these components are \( O\left( {\left( {\left| \mathcal{U}\right| + \left| {\mathcal{I}}^{A}\right| + \left| {\mathcal{I}}^{B}\right| }\right) \cdot d}\right) ,O\left( {{4d} \cdot \left( {d + 1}\right) }\right) ,O\left( {P \cdot d}\right) \) ,and \( O\left( {{16d} \cdot \left( {{4d} + 1}\right) + 1}\right) \) ,respectively. Here, \( d \) denotes the embedding size,and \( P \) represents the number of experts in the MoE architecture. Given that \( \left| \mathcal{U}\right| ,\left| {\mathcal{I}}^{A}\right| \) ,and \( \left| {\mathcal{I}}^{B}\right| \) are significantly larger than \( d \) and \( P \) ,the overall space complexity of KDCLM can be approximated as \( O\left( {\left( {\left| \mathcal{U}\right| + \left| {\mathcal{I}}^{A}\right| + \left| {\mathcal{I}}^{B}\right| }\right) \cdot d + {4d} \cdot \left( {d + 1}\right) + P \cdot d + {16d} \cdot \left( {{4d} + 1}\right) + 1}\right) \approxeq \; O\left( {\left( {\left| \mathcal{U}\right| + \left| {\mathcal{I}}^{A}\right| + \left| {\mathcal{I}}^{B}\right| }\right) \cdot d}\right) \) . This complexity is on the same order as that of most existing CDR methods, indicating that KDCLM is scalable and efficient in terms of space usage. 5.2.2 Time Complexity. The time complexity of the KDCLM model arises from the following components: (1) Graph Convolution Operation: This process requires \( O\left( {L \cdot N \cdot k \cdot d}\right) \) time complexity to learn representations on each graph,where \( N \) is the number of nodes, \( k \) is the average number of neighbors per node, \( d \) is the embedding size,and \( L \) is the number of graph convolution layers. (2) Representation Disentanglement Module: This module first involves generating separate representations with a time complexity of \( O\left( {d}^{2}\right) \) . Subsequently,it requires \( O\left( {P \cdot {N}^{2} \cdot d}\right) \) for neighbor identification, \( O\left( {{N}^{2} \cdot d}\right) \) for calculating the instance-level contrastive learning loss,and \( O\left( {{N}^{2} \cdot d}\right) \) for calculating the feature-level contrastive learning loss. Thus, the total time complexity for this module is \( O\left( {{d}^{2} + P \cdot {N}^{2} \cdot d}\right) \) . (3) Graph Knowledge Enhancement Module: This component has a time complexity of \( O\left( {N \cdot k \cdot d}\right) \) . (4) Prediction Score Generation and Recommendation Loss Calculation: This step involves generating predicted scores and calculating the recommendation loss, with a time complexity of \( O\left( {N \cdot k \cdot {d}^{2}}\right) \) .

Based on the above analysis,the total time complexity of the proposed KDCLM model is \( O(L \cdot \; N \cdot k \cdot d + P \cdot {N}^{2} \cdot d + N \cdot k \cdot {d}^{2} \) ). Given the following relationships in our model: \( L < d \) (the number of graph convolution layers is less than the embedding size); \( P < d \) (the number of experts is less than the embedding size); \( k < < N \) (the average number of neighbors is much smaller than the total number of nodes due to graph sparsity). Thus, the overall time complexity of KDCLM can be simplified to \( O\left( {P \cdot {N}^{2} \cdot d}\right) \) ,which is approximately \( O\left( {N}^{2}\right) \) . ### 5.3 Extension to Multi-Domain Scenarios Our proposed method KDCLM can naturally scale to multi-domain scenarios. Let \( {D}^{1},{D}^{2},\ldots ,{D}^{K} \) denote \( K \) different domains. For the local view,for every domain \( {D}^{k} \) ,we still construct a local interaction graph \( {G}^{k}\left( {{V}^{k},{E}^{k}}\right) \) and generate a domain-invariant and a domain-specific user representation. For alignment of domain-invariant representations, the neighbor-discrimination contrastive learning objective will treat the domain-invariant representations of the same (or similar) user coming from any two domains as a positive pair, whereas representations of dissimilar users across domains form negative pairs. For the differentiation of domain-specific representations, the feature-level contrastive learning objective will emphasize feature-wise diversity between a user's domain-specific representations of any two distinct domains. For the global view, we construct a unified user-item interaction graph \( {G}^{UI} = \left( {{V}^{UI},{E}^{UI}}\right) \) ,a user-user similarity graph \( {G}^{UU} = \left( {{V}^{UU},{E}^{UU}}\right) \) , and an item-item relationship graph \( {G}^{II} = \left( {{V}^{II},{E}^{II}}\right) \) based on interactions from all \( K \) domains. Graph convolution and the graph knowledge enhancement are then performed exactly as in the two-domain setting. For the prediction layer, it is the same as when there are two domains. For model optimization,the loss function is a joint loss on all domains,that is, \( \mathcal{L} = \mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{K}{\mathcal{L}}_{CE}^{k} + \; {\lambda }_{1}\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{K}{\mathcal{L}}_{KD}^{k}}\right) + {\lambda }_{2}\left( {\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{k = 1}}^{K}{\mathcal{L}}_{C{L}_{a}}^{k} + {\mathcal{L}}_{C{L}_{d}}}\right) + {\lambda }_{3}\parallel \Theta {\parallel }_{2}^{2}. \) ## 6 Experiments In this section, we conduct extensive experiments on four real-world CDR tasks to address the following research questions: -How does the proposed KDCLM model perform compared to state-of-the-art single-domain and cross-domain methods? - To what extent do the key designs (e.g., the domain-invariant representation alignment mechanism, the domain-specific representation differentiation mechanism, and the graph knowledge enhancement module) contribute to the model's performance? -How does KDCLM perform at different sparsity levels and user-overlapping ratios? -How do the key hyper-parameters (e.g., the KD loss weight, the contrastive loss weight, the softmax temperature, the number of GCN layers and the warm-up epochs) impact the performance of our model?

To evaluate the performance of our proposed KDCLM model, we conduct extensive experiments on two widely used CDR datasets: the Amazon dataset \( {}^{1} \) and the Douban dataset. \( {}^{2} \) For Amazon,we selected three domains that have been extensively studied in prior works [31, 38, 40, 66], namely "CDs and Vinyl," "Movies and TV," and "Books." We define three CDR tasks by pairing these domains: "Amazon-Movies \( \leftrightarrow \) Amazon-CDs," "Amazon-Books \( \leftrightarrow \) Amazon-CDs," and "Amazon-Books \( \leftrightarrow \) Amazon-Movies." For each domain,ratings of 4 or 5 were treated as positive samples. For Douban, we focused on the "Douban-Books \( \leftrightarrow \) Douban-Movies" task. In both datasets, users and items with fewer than five interactions were filtered out. Additionally, we randomly retained 10,000 items for each Douban domain to control the dataset size. Detailed statistics of the datasets are summarized in Table 2. 6.1.2 Evaluation Metrics. When assessing model efficacy, we adopt a broadly recognized ranking-based evaluation strategy: the leave-one-out evaluation protocol [80]. For each user, we reserve one interaction as the test item and determine hyper-parameters by randomly sampling another interaction as the validation set. The remaining interactions are used for training. We evaluate performance using two metrics: Hit Ratio (HR) and Normalized Discounted Cumulative Gain (NDCG). HR@N assesses whether the test item appears within the top- \( N \) ranked items while NDCG@N evaluates the quality of the ranking, assigning higher scores to hits in higher positions: \[{HR}@N = \frac{1}{\left| {U}_{t}\right| }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i \in {U}_{t}}}\delta \left( {{p}_{i} \leq \operatorname{top}N}\right) ,\;{NDCG}@N = \frac{1}{\left| {U}_{t}\right| }\mathop{\sum }\limits_{{i \in {U}_{t}}}\frac{\log 2}{\log \left( {{p}_{i} + 1}\right) }, \tag{16}\] where \( {U}_{t} \) denotes the set of test samples, \( {p}_{i} \) is the position of the test item for user \( i \) ,and \( \delta \left( \cdot \right) \) is the indicator function. For both metrics, a higher value indicates superior performance. We empirically set \( N \) to 5 and 10 . 6.1.3 Comparison Methods. - DGCF [58]: This method considers user-item relationships at a finer granularity by focusing on user intents. A neighbor routing mechanism exploits node-neighbor affinity to refine intent-aware graphs, and embedding propagation on these graphs updates nodes' intent-aware embeddings. - SGL [62]: This method leverages the strengths of contrastive learning by introducing three data augmentation operations-node dropout, edge dropout, and random walk-to generate multiple views for each node. Node self-discrimination is used as a self-supervised task to provide auxiliary signals for representation learning. - RecDCL [75]: This method combines feature-wise and batch-wise contrastive learning objectives for self-supervised recommendations. The joint training objectives eliminate redundancy between users and items and enhance the robustness of the representations. - A-LLMRec [23]: This method devises an alignment network that aligns the item embeddings of the collaborative filtering recommender system with the token space of the LLM, aiming at transferring the collaborative knowledge to the LLM. (2) CDR Methods. - CMF [51]: This method collectively factorizes interaction matrices from both domains and shares latent factors of overlapping entities (users or items) across domains to facilitate knowledge transfer. - Bi-TGCF [37]: This bi-directional transfer learning method uses a graph collaborative filtering network as its base model. It proposes a knowledge transfer module to extend the flow of features from in-domain to inter-domain and integrates users' common features with domain-specific features. - DisenCDR [5]: This deep generative model follows the variational autoencoder framework to model data distributions. It introduces a variational bipartite graph encoder and two mutual-information-based regularizers-an exclusive regularizer and an informative regularizer-to disentangle users' domain-shared and domain-specific representations. - UniCDR [4]: This unified model transfers domain-shared information across diverse CDR scenarios. It uses interaction and domain masking mechanisms to produce augmented data and constrains the domain-shared representation to encode invariant information through a contrastive loss. - GDCCDR [35]: This method employs an adaptive, parameter-free filter in graph convolution to gauge interaction significance based on user-item similarity when generating disentangled features. It also utilizes meta-networks to facilitate the personalized transfer of domain-invariant features. - CiUT [27]: This method proposes the collaborative information regularized user transformation to alleviate negative transfer resulting from distortion of user similarity relationships by adding constraints to filter irrelevant user collaborative information. - PicCDR [54]: This method utilizes textual semantics to disentangle and enhance domain-invariant and domain-specific representations via LLMs with a contrastive domain-disentangled augmentation strategy. 6.1.4 Experimental Setup. We implemented the KDCLM model using PyTorch, with all experiments conducted on an NVIDIA A40 GPU. The embedding dimension for users and items was set to 64 in both global and local views. We applied a stack of two graph convolution layers to all constructed graphs. (3) w/o.kd, which removes the KD loss, deactivating knowledge transfer between graph signals of distinct global graphs. (4) w/o.fcl, which excludes the feature-level contrastive learning mechanism, ignoring the differentiation of domain-specific representations. (5) w/o.icl, which omits the instance-level contrastive learning mechanism, overlooking the alignment of domain-invariant representations. (6) w/o.inv, which removes the domain-invariant representations and only the domain-specific component is retained. (7) w/o.spe, which removes the domain-specific representations and retains only the domain-invariant component. (8) w/o.mg, which constructs a joint graph that merges all edges in the global heterogeneous and homogeneous graphs. (9) w/o.MoE, which removes the MoEs mechanism by reducing the number of experts to 1. The results are shown in Figure 4. Removing the global view results in a 2.08% drop on the "Amazon-Movies \( \leftrightarrow \) Amazon-CDs" task and a 8.67% decrease on the "Douban-Books \( \leftrightarrow \) Douban-Movies" task. The removal of the KD loss also leads to notable performance drops, with an average reduction of 3.02% and 6.56% on the two tasks, proving the effectiveness of transferring sufficient knowledge embedded within the global graph signals. These investigations provide deeper insights into how each hyper-parameter contributes to the overall performance and benefit the determination of optimal parameter settings. 6.6.1 Impact of the KD Loss Weight \( {\lambda }_{1} \) . The KD loss weight \( {\lambda }_{1} \) in Equation (15) determines the proportion of the KD loss,i.e., \( {\mathcal{L}}_{KD}^{A} \) and \( {\mathcal{L}}_{KD}^{B} \) within the overall loss function. To evaluate its impact,we varied \( {\lambda }_{1} \) across \( \{ 0,{0.1},{0.5},{1.0},{2.0}\} \) and assessed the model performance on HR@10 and NDCG@10.The results are illustrated in Figure 7(a). The results indicate that as \( {\lambda }_{1} \) increases from 0 (no KD) to 0.1, the model performance improves by 1.20% and 2.78% in terms of HR@10, respectively. However,when \( {\lambda }_{1} \) takes on higher values (e.g., \( {\lambda }_{1} = 1 \) or \( {\lambda }_{1} = 2 \) ),the model performance degrades in both domains. This decline is primarily due to an excessive focus on KD, which overshadows the predominant recommendation loss and leads to suboptimal representation learning. In summary, \( {\lambda }_{1} = {0.5} \) strikes the optimal balance,allowing the model to facilitate sufficient knowledge transfer in the global view while bringing the recommendation loss constraint into full play. 6.6.2 Impact of the Contrastive Loss Weight \( {\lambda }_{2} \) . The contrastive learning loss weight \( {\lambda }_{2} \) in Equation (15) determines the proportion of the instance-level and feature-level contrastive learning losses in the overall loss function. To investigate its impact,we conduct experiments with \( {\lambda }_{2} \) values from \( \{ 0,{0.0001},{0.001},{0.01},{0.1}\} \) and analyze its influence on model performance. The experimental results are visualized in Figure 7(b), which illustrates HR@10 and NDCG@10 across different values of \( {\lambda }_{2} \) . As observed from the results,increasing \( {\lambda }_{2} \) from 0 to 0.001 leads to significant improvements in both HR@10 and NDCG@10 across domains, with gains of 3.37% and 5.18%, respectively. This demonstrates that the incorporation of contrastive learning effectively benefit model performance improvements. However,as \( {\lambda }_{2} \) increases beyond 0.001,model performance begins to degrade. Notably,when \( {\lambda }_{2} = {0.1} \) ,HR@10 decreases by 8.07% and 10.71% while NDCG@10 decreases by 7.40% and 4.91%, suggesting that an overly strong contrastive learning objective may force excessive alignment of user domain-invariant representations while amplifying the distinctions between user domain-specific features, ultimately disrupting the balance needed for effective recommendations. These findings highlight the importance of appropriately balancing contrastive learning loss and recommendation loss to achieve optimal model performance.

6.6.3 Impact of the Softmax Temperature \( \tau \) . The softmax temperature \( \tau \) is a crucial hyper-parameter in contrastive learning, as it amplifies the effect of constraints and adjusts the model's sensitivity to similarity calculations. To evaluate its impact, we conduct experiments with different temperature values \( \{ {0.01},{0.05},{0.1},{0.5},{1.0}\} \) ,and the results are shown in Figure 7(c). The results indicate that the model achieves the best performance across both domains when \( \tau = {0.1} \) ,as \( \tau \) increases from 0.1 to 1, the HR@10 performance slightly declines by 1.37% and 1.48%, respectively, though it remains close to the peak values. Conversely,when \( \tau \) falls below 0.1,HR@5 performance declines by 2.29% and 1.52%,respectively, indicating that extreme similarity scores lead to overemphasize a limited subset of negative samples while neglecting overall feature generalization. Nevertheless, since the performance variation across different temperature settings is relatively minor, these results further confirm the model's robustness and adaptability. 6.6.4 Impact of the Number of GCN Layers. Overall, these results highlight that two layers strike an optimal balance between capturing higher-order information and maintaining representation quality as well as avoiding overfitting. 6.6.5 Impact of the Warm-Up Epochs. In our proposed model, during the warm-up phase, we identify each user's neighbors based solely on behavioral similarity, excluding embedding similarity. The epoch of the warm-up phase determines when embedding similarity will be incorporated into the neighbor identification process. To assess its impact, we conduct experiments with different numbers of warm-up epochs \( \{ 0,{10},{20},{30},{40},{50}\} \) ,and the results are presented in Figure 9. As training progresses and the epoch increases to 20, the model's performance steadily improves, with HR@10 and NDCG@10 increasing by an average of 4.28% and 2.51%, respectively. Therefore, setting the warm-up epochs to 20 provides an optimal balance, ensuring that the model benefits from both well-initialized embeddings and adaptive user similarity learning.

We will investigate dynamic graph construction techniques that can adapt to evolving user preferences and item characteristics over time.
